vyādhi
(‘disease’)
------------------------------------------
Āyurveda or the science of health and longevity, categorises व्याधि or roga (disease) into four groups: āgantuka (coming from external sources or accidents); śārīra (arising in the body due to the disturbance of the balance of the three हुमोउर्स् viz., kapha, vāta and pitta); mānasa (of the मिन्द्, due to jealousy, anger, lust and so on); svābhāvika (natural due to hunger, thirst, oldage, sleep etc.).
These diseases may be caused by faulty living as also by the कर्म of the previous lives.
See also ĀDHI and ĀYURVEDA.

vyāhṛtihoma
(‘homa (with the utterance of the] व्याहृतिस्’)
------------------------------------------
The व्याहृतिहोम is done during उपनयन and some other minor rites like सीमन्तोन्नयन (parting of the hair upwards, of the pregnant wife).
The three words bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ and svaḥ or suvaḥ are called व्याहृतिस् and are generally added at the beginning of the Gāyatrīmantra.
In the व्याहृतिहोम, oblations of clarified butter are given to the accom-paniment of the व्याहृतिस् pronounced singly, and then, together.

vyāghāta
(‘[a statement that] contradicts itself’)
------------------------------------------
Vyāghāta is listed as one of the eleven kinds of तर्क or लोगिच्. It is actually a statement that contradicts itself and hence ridiculous.
An interesting stanza sometimes quoted by commentators runs as follows: (A person is telling his friend) ‘Throughout my life I have been dumb. My ड़थेर् is a celibate. My मोथेर् is a barren woman. My grandfather was without children!’

Vyavahāra-mayūkha
------------------------------------------
This is a digest of civil law written by Nīlakaṇṭhabhaṭṭa (17th century A. D.).
See BHAGAVANTA-BHĀSKARA.

Vyāsasmṛti
------------------------------------------
Vyāsa—also known as कृष्ण Dvaipā-yana and Vedavyāsa—is the reputed author of the epic Mahābhārata and also the पुराणस्. However, the Vyāsasmṛti as available now in print is a work of another व्यास who might have lived during the period A.

-500. He might have been a contemporary of other writers of smṛtis like बृहस्पति and याज्ञवल्क्य.
The printed text as available now has 250 verses and deals with the following topics: extent of the land where the dharmas described here apply; relative authoritativeness of the Śruti, स्मृति and the पुराणस्; mixed castes; the sixteen सṁस्कारस्; duties of a ब्रह्मचारिन्; duties of a wife; नित्य, naimittika and kāmya karmas of a householder; on gifts.
Other well-known writers on the dharmaśāstra often quote verses as of व्यास. These are mostly from the Mahā-bhārata. There are also verses not found in the epic. These verses—about 200 in number—deal with the topic of vyavahāra or common laws. Quite a few legal matters bearing on gifts of land, procedures in lawsuits and division of ancestral property are dealt with in these verses. The topic of śrāddha (obsequial rites) is also touched upon.

vyasana
(‘that which deprives a person [from great good]’)
------------------------------------------
The position of the king or the ruler of a country involves a heavy responsibility. The life and property of its people, their religion and culture, the natural resources—in fact, every aspect of the nation’s life—depends upon him. If he is a good and great king, the country will prosper. If not, it will suffer much.
Hindu religious works list a number of vyasanas or vices of a king that lead to his fall and ruin his country.
The vices in his personal life are mainly four: pāna (drinking); akṣa or द्यूत (gambling); स्त्री (sexual excesses); mṛgayā (hunting). Some of the other defects are: wrong policy decisions; harshness of speech; excessive use of force; mismanagement of financial resources; neglecting his duties and responsibilities.
Kauṭilya (321 B. C.) in his monumental work, the Arthaśāstra (Chapter 8) discusses the topic of व्यसन in great detail. Some of the natural disasters like अग्नि (fire), durbhikṣa (famine) and ativṛṣṭi (floods) have also been listed as vyasanas.
There can be vyasanas or defects in other fields of the kingdom also, such as amātyas (ministers), jana (people of the country), durga (fort), बल (armed forces) and so on.

vyākaraṇa
(‘[a science] that makes [language] more clear,’ ‘grammar’)
------------------------------------------
Vyākaraṇa or grammar is one of the six वेदाङ्गस् or subsidiaries of the Veda. It is described as the face or the mouth of the Vedapuruṣa, the Veda personified as the cosmic being.
Some scholars feel that there is a clear reference to व्याकरण in the Ṛgvedic मन्त्र 4.58.6 which compares it to a vṛṣabha or a bull. Nāma (noun), ākhyāta (verb), upasarga (prefix) and so on, are its various limbs. However others do not agree with this view.
Another मन्त्र of the Ṛgveda (10.71.4) praises व्याकरण since it helps one to understand the purport of the वेदस् correctly.
The Gopatha Brāhmaṇa (1.24) of the Atharvaveda mentions most of the technical terms commonly used in Sanskrit grammar.
Vararuci (58 B. C.) has delineated five uses of grammar. They are: rakṣā (protection of the वेदस्); ūhā (guessing the correct meaning of the Vedic sentences, especially those concerned with yāgas or sacrifices); āgama (Vedic statements supporting the study of grammar); laghu (suggesting an easy way of attaining our wishes by understanding the वेदस् properly); asandeha (clearing the doubts of the Vedic sentences).
Which exactly is the original व्याकरण considered the Vedāṅga, is difficult to say. Though an Aindra-vyākaraṇa is alluded to in the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (

.3) as a very ancient work of grammar, it is not available now in any form. Among the extant vyākaraṇas, पाणिनि’s Aṣṭādhyāyī is the earliest (500 B. C.). However, it refers to several grammarians of the earlier period. Some of them are: Āpiśalī (

).
For all practical purposes, the Aṣṭādhyāyī of पाणिनि may be taken as the Vedāṅga-व्याकरण.
The Aṣṭādhyāyī deals with both Vedic Sanskrit and classical Sanskrit. (See AṢṬĀDHYĀYĪ for more details.)
This work has several commentaries. The Mahābhāṣya of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) is the most celebrated of them all. The Vārttika of कात्यायन which is incomplete, is another well-known work. The Kāśikā-वृत्ति of वामन and Jayāditya (A.

) is a brief but complete commentary on पाणिनि.
Another well-known work which is extremely popular even now is the Siddhāntakaumudī of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita (A.

-1650). This is a rearrangement of all the sūtras of पाणिनि according to the subject matter, with his own gloss. वरदराज, his disciple, prepared two more shorter versions—the Madhya-सिद्धान्त-kaumudī and the Laghusiddhāntakaumudī—which too are popular even to this day.
In the post-पाणिनि period, several schools of grammar evolved, based upon some important basic works. Six of them may be mentioned here: the Kātantra school of Śarvavarma (1st century A. D.); the Cāndra-व्याकरण school of चन्द्र-gomiya (5th century A. D.); the Jainendra व्याकरण school of Devanandin (6th century A. D.); the Śākaṭāyana व्याकरण school of Pālyakīrti (9th century A. D.); the Siddha Hemacandra school or Haima व्याकरण school of Hemacandrasūri (12th century A. D.); the सरस्वती-kaṇṭhā-bharaṇa school of the Paramāra king भोज (11th century A. D.).
Some of the other grammatical works of the later period are: the Saṅkṣiptasāra of Kramadīśvara (12th century A. D.); the Mugdhabodha of बोपदेव (13th century A. D.); the Supadmavyākaraṇa of पद्म-nābha (A.

) and Sārasvata-vyākaraṇa of Anubhūtisvarūpa (14th century A. D.).
Mention may be made here of the treatises dealing exclusively with the genders of nouns, a class of literature known as Liṅgānuśāsanas. Of all such works, the Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana of Amara-siṁha (A.

) is the best known and most widely used.
It may also be noted that some ancient grammarians like पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) and भर्तृहरि (A.

-500) have developed a spiritual philosophy out of grammar, identifying the eternal aspect of sound (= nityaśabda) with the ब्रह्मन् of Vedānta.
The following are the subjects normally dealt with in all these works of grammar:
Nāmapada (nouns); sarvanāma (pronouns); लिङ्ग (gender); vacana (number); vibhakti (declension); धातु (root-verbs); kriyāpada (verbs and their forms according to tenses and moods); avyaya (indeclinables); taddhitānta (words derived from nouns); kṛdanta (words derived from verbs).

vyabhicāra
(‘transgression’)
------------------------------------------
In general it means an evil act and in particular, अदुल्तेर्य्. The धर्मशास्त्रस् prescribe various kinds of punishment like amputation or even death.
In लोगिच् it means a fallacy. If an effect is denied even though the cause exists, or, if an effect is accepted to exist in spite of the fact that the cause does not, it becomes the fallacy of व्यभिचार.

-1539)
------------------------------------------
Vyāsatīrtha—also known as व्यास-rāya—was one of the brightest personalities of Karnataka who shone not only as a great scholar-saint but also as an able administrator of the Vijayanagar empire.
Born in A.

as the son of Rāmācārya and Lakṣmīdevī at Abbūr in the Mysore district of Karnataka, he was initiated into सṁन्यास by Brahmaṇya-tīrtha, with the monastic name of व्यासतीर्थ. He learnt all the scriptures under another great सोउल् Śrīpādarāya (d. A.

).
He toured the country extensively and established his reputation as a great scholar, unexcelled in philosophical disputations. He was the rājaguru (royal preceptor) to five generations of kings of Vijayanagar. He is said to have saved the king Kṛṣṇadevarāya (A.

-1529) from the kuhūyoga, an extremely inauspicious (astrological) moment, dangerous for rulers.
He organised the rituals of the temples of तिरुमल-तिरुपति for twelve years and then handed it over to the hereditary successors of the priests of the deity.
He established 732 images of Māruti (Hanumān) in several parts of the country.
His well-known works of द्वैत Vedānta are: Nyāyāmṛta, Tarkatāṇḍava and Tātparyacandrikā.
He has also composed many devotional songs in Kannada with the pseudonym श्रीकृष्ण.
Purandaradāsa (A.

-1606), the two famous saint-musicians of Karnataka were his disciples.
The मठ (monastery) he had established at Sosale in the Mysore district is still in existence.
